game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is fantastic.  It takes the themes expressed in Orwell's 1984 and allows you to take a "big brother" role by reading through social media to decide who is responsible for a series events thought to be done by terrorists.  I was on the edge of my seat the whole time, and it also made me think about every action I took.  Did I want to mark this suspect as potentially dangerous based on an altercation she got into a long time ago?  Is this article an accurate depiction of the person she is now?  Actions like these will come back to haunt you based on the outcomes later in the game.  

Overall, my only complaint with this game is that the ending felt a little too abrupt.  The game is episodic, and the final episode was significantly shorter than every other episode.  Overall, though, I would highly recommend picking this game up.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"The thoughts are free" ... or are they?

Orwell is a pretty neat little game about the potential dangers of openly accessible (or even not so openly accessible) data and the connections and conclusions you can draw from them.

You start out as an investigator for the project "Orwell", a surveillance system meant to protect the people and prevent crimes. 
After a bombing attack you are tasked, together with your supervisor, to find out who was behind the bombings and to prevent further ones.
As you dig deeper through websites and files, desktops and other material, you'll uncover more and more of the story, the motivations of the people responsible for the bombings and uncover some twists and turns throughout your investigations.

The gameplay is pretty simplistic. It's pretty much like surfing through a browser. You can access (predefined) websites and read through articles, blogs and also social media. Throughout the text you find some marked passages, which will help you with your investigation. You can connect these infos with a person and send these infos to Orwell. You can also decide to withhold some informations, letting events turn out differently in the process.

The story and events really sucked me in and were pretty thrilling. Slowly finding out more about the people, their connections to each other, and also be suprised by some twists, made the game very entertaining.

So if you don't mind simplistic gameplay and reading quite a lot and and the topic of data security doesn't turn you down, this is a little gem to keep an eye on.

I'd definitely recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm speechless as in what to say for this game, since the entire story totally got me so hard that I'm quite sad it's >only< 5 hours long.

I had quite high expectations, considering the price of the game and the game's length, and I'm very happy to say that Orwell didn't disappoint, not even a little. Episode 1, which is also included in the demo is very short and serves more like a "tutorial" than actual gameplay, and after completing it I was afraid that the rest would look similar - nothing like that, all other 4 episodes were so intense and well-written that I immediately went back to my previous happy state and enjoyed my fun.

And believe me - I hate all sort of VNs and games with huge amount of text, they're usually boring for me and I quickly lose my interest, that's why I was a bit sceptical at first whether I'm going to enjoy Orwell, but I decided to go with it due to a nice -43% (bundle) discount, and I can say that the experience is well worth the money, even at full price.

You should DEFINITELY grab the game if you're interested in all sort of government spying on people, but apart from that it'd be also interesting position for people interested in "working" for government in general, doing detective work, connecting various pieces together and enjoying awesome story. In fact, the story is the most polished thing in the entire game, and it's alone worth the time and money spent on the title, that's why I'd recommend this title even for people that expect more gameplay than reading, such as myself.

From the bad things, the game can seem a bit too "casual", especially for more oldschool gamers like myself - I'd appreciate difficulty setting that would turn off highlighting relevant facts, and definitely allow to jump onto conclusions with only half-available data. Don't get me wrong - the game is awesome and those are not any crucial things that would heavily affect the gameplay, but I kinda miss the option of actually "losing", by jumping onto false assumption and getting fired. Losing should definitely be an option here.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time, this is at least a 9/10 from me - missing point only for being too casual, although that didn't stop me from enjoying the awesome story that the devs coded for me, since I had a lot of fun. I can definitely recommend the title to everyone!

review_text_raw: This is an excellent game.  I went into it fully expecting it to be about the evils of government surveillance, and that you would see first hand the terrible effects and repercussions that it will bring.  Instead I got a very nuanced storyline that presented both sides of the issue, leaving you wondering afterwards if perhaps there is a practical middle ground that can be sought.  The gameplay is also very addictive and unique, and there are several endings depending on your choices, with lots of little twists and turns.  The game is very intelligent in regards to making your choices make a huge difference in the outcome, even if you think the ones you pick are not that important in the grand scheme of things.  One of the best titles I played this past year. Highly recommended.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Welcome to Orwellian Big Brother where every action by every citizen of "The Nation" is captured and recorded, and where citizens can be arrested for even the slightest transgression or declaration of anti-Orwell thoughts against The Nation.  You have been recruited by the government as one of its anonymous investigators who must dissect pertinent data and upload this to the government affiliate working with you to prevent a series of terrorist attacks that have been taking place.  Your affiliate can only act on the information you provide (they have no access to the information you have) so your choices matter!

The interface is a joy: very simple and clean, everything very obvious, and the game leads in with a simple tutorial to introduce you to your three tools of Orwell.  On one side of the screen you can open a person's profile to see what information you've gathered on them, and on the other will be their calls messages and mail, with potentially-relevant text highlighted in blue for you to choose whether to add to a person's profile (it cannot be undone if you make a mistake).  You will have to discern who's telling the truth or not, and sometimes you don't have enough information to be 100% sure.  Drag information to a person's profile to attach it to them, and hope you've made the right decision because there is no way to undo this action.

The game would best be described as a combination of simulation, visual novel and point-and-click, but it carries none of the downsides of these games.  Any reading to be done is short, brief and well written, it's really simple to play, and what you can click on is limited to small nuggets of information that the Orwell system deems potentially relevant (and you must decide whether this will help or hinder the government in thwarting the terrorism).  It's not a difficult game, but it's gripping and all too easy to implicate the wrong individual.  At the end I saw the mistakes I'd made.  The best of it is that I somehow suspected that some information was not right as I was playing, but felt compelled to upload it anyway!  My bad!  Replayability is there because there are different outcomes along the way.  The ending is huge but I cannot tell you a thing about it without spoiling the game, but it is worth reaching.

And the soundtrack is amazing.  It's the first time I've ever bought a soundtrack for a game!

If you're unsure, there is a separate playable demo (that's what convinced me to buy the game) and I'm so glad I did.  Yet another great hit for an Indie team who also made the marvellous Hacknet game.  I can't wait to see what Osmotic Studios produce next.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer. All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed. One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead. Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting. In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels. Stay vigilant.

review_text_raw:
[h1]General[/h1]

This is [b]not really a game.[/b] Most of the time you would only be pointing out "data chunks" to relevant character, and the said data chunks has been conveniently pointed out to you by the highlight, so you can't miss it. The only time you get a little pressure is on the final episode, when there are "data upload" limit imposed on you.

[h1]There is minimal gameplay[/h1]
There is minimal gameplay, as it is mostly just drag and drop something. The clues are too easily pointed out to you. Sometimes there are some conflicting data, but it is easy to resolve this kind of things. It is also bad that you don't know how the data chunks you are given is processed. A wrong data chunk could suddenly net a very violent response although previous data chunks you have given it is not the way. 


[h1]Story-Rich Gameplay[/h1]
However, the story in the game is excellent. It is not overly long and complicated, but it is quite complicated enough to keep you guessing on who is who and what is the truth beneath all of these things. All of the characters are alive, and the way they are chatting with each other, with you snooping in, at times make you guilty for snooping on someone's conversation. You will also see another person's life, and at times you will feel guilty that you are the one that send them into prison, sometimes by bending the truth so they can be arrested. And seeing their hobbies and their life, but watching their conversation, their blogs, or their social medias, sometimes makes you really hopeful that this guy/girl is not guilty so you could release them, and make you guilty if you have to arrest them.

[h1]Politics and Mass Surveillance[/h1]
Of course, this game is quite a political game, on the issue of mass surveillance. It subtly asks the player on how far the government could go in the name of security, and how is privacy should be treated if you have connection with a terror group. The game beautifully does not refer to any country or any political party (though a subtle jab at "Freedom" and "Peacekeeping" is done). 

Overall a beautiful game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Big Brother watches you. That’s what they told us back in the days, when it was just some kinda fiction and a fantastic story. Now, in our present times this issue has become like a real problem, especially for someone who believes, that their lives are important as hell and like to play a private card all the time. 

The government can learn about you literally everything, thanks to social media, your online purchases, all the cameras hanging around the city, watching at you, information you provide to your employers when you attend to job, mobile phones you use with a GPS modules, etc. 

It can be a problem for lots of people, especially for some who is paranoid and doesn’t seem to be busy all the time with any kind of work (because, otherwise, they wouldn’t have time for these kind of thoughts). On the other hand, it can be really helpful to identify a threat and prevent some kind of tragedy from a single murder to a massive terrorist attack.

Orwell try to develop this idea. In this game, which presents as a visual novel with its own dystopia universe, you have to identify the threat. You will do this with the help of Orwell, a program, created for surveilling the citizens. The whole job starts when system marks someone as a potential threat and you have to investigate that person. Usually, it all starts kinda mild and innocent - you check the public records and information, that does not require you to spy on someone or even hack it - you will check newspapers, police records, maybe some websites. However, in most situations it’s not enough and you have to dig deeper, checking private emails, phonebooks, chat logs, listening to phone calls all other kind of intrusion to private life.

So,what’s the whole point of the game? While you checking on person’s information - Orwell will highlight the most important parts, regarding your investigation. And your task is to gather all of them into one piece for every profile, every person. If you are doubt in the information you’ll have to disable it, or simply ignore it. For example you found a statement about your victim in some kinda boulevard newspaper - definitely not trustworthy source and if it conflicts with another info you found earlier it will be highlighted with a yellow color. So, it’s up to you, to choose where is the truth and where is the misleading information. But you should keep in mind, that you are the one who is responsible for what will happen next to this person, so be responsible for your actions.

And that’s what made Orwell so interesting to me - I literally wanted to find the real truth, you know, to investigate this to the fullest. I never had this feeling, like yeah yeah yeah whatever, I put this metadata here, this one there, oh, a conflict? Lol, whatever, just let me finish this game. No, it wasn’t this case. I felt like I was so into the cases, to understand, either I am dealing with a real threat, a terrorist, or maybe we just ran into something really serious, where someone tries to set up a complete innocent guy and maybe I should pay more attention here and re-check all the profiles. So, Orwell is more about investigation and your ability to read between the lines where it’s needed.

At this point, some of the players will understand that this is not their type of game. Like it or not, but you seriously can’t control the situation, you can’t change something, can’t help to prevent the damage, which is about to happen. You just simply have to put facts in a right place with a right persons and listen to the comments of your mentor Symes. That guy is simply ridiculous. It starts as a tutorial guy at the start of the game, who has to show you all the basics and teach you how to play, and then after that it stays there for the game to react on your actions. Basically, it doesn’t have any access to the information you gathered, so it can only comment on the newest information you provided and by these comments you have to understand either you move the right or a shallow way. 

Orwell is definitely a blast. It has this unique kind of a gameplay with its deep idea and rich stories for someone, who truly values games as a real art. The combination of twists, turnabouts and all these thrilling moments make this game a great place to spend a few hours, maybe dozens of hours, if you will feel like having more than one run to reveal all the achievements and endings. 

Okay, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:

+ Conspiracy theory lover
+ Love the idea of investigating and matching data and clues into one piece 
+ You want to entertain yourself in a great story game for at least few hours
+ Like to dig to the bottom to find out who is who
+ Fan of dramatic stories with its twists, thrilling moments and surprises

Recommend to avoid if you:

- Don’t get the idea of visual novel
- Not a fan of all these talks that government spy on you and we are all under control.  

Enjoy!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The game starts very simply:
There was a terror attack, and it’s up to you to investigate all available sources to discover who is responsible.
Basically detective work in the 21st century.
But as the game progresses, you discover there is much more than meets the eye.
Not only the suspects you track, their actions and relationships, but also your actions, and those of your superiors, all become important.
You start off as a mere spectator, but even by witnessing the events, you are already impacting them.
And once you realize your impact on the world you were meant to observe, you’re now faced with difficult choices.
Choices that are not right or wrong - only choices you need live with for the rest of your life…

This is a really good game, that dives deep into questions of terror, accountability, privacy, and more.

The only issue I had with this game, is that even though you don’t have to submit every single piece of evidence you find.
And can be even reprimanded for submitting irrelevant evidence,
The game simply refuses to progress until you submit almost every piece.
For example:
Let’s say you discover a person likes strawberry ice cream. But that has nothing to do with determining if he’s a terrorist or not, so you ignore this piece of info (mark it as ignored).
Then nothing happens. The game simply refuses to progress any further.
So you submit the only remaining piece of info, that the suspect likes strawberry ice cream, and like clockwork, you’re immediately reprimanded by your superior that this piece of data has nothing to do with the case at hand (daaa….).
But then suddenly the suspect receives an incriminating phone call - and the game suddenly starts progressing.

So instead of submitting useless data being a trigger to game progression, simply marking the data as “ignored” should serve the same purpose.

Other than that - it’s a really good game.
Much better than it’s sequel (Ignorance is Strength)

review_text_raw:
Great game, I got it in the humble bundle monthly along with other games, and decided to play it because it looked interesting.

Describing the game, it's a very well made point and click adventure, but it's different from your typical point and click games because here you just use Orwell, an operating system designed to watch and monitor people, you can browse different websites and access all sorts of public and private information about your suspects, you go from page to page, phone to phone, computer to computer, device to device, as you try and look for useful information that may help you in your objectives.

The story is short but entertaining and exciting, you get the feeling of really becoming an Orwell 'investigator', the feeling is authentic, the websites, pages, profiles, articles, and that sort of stuff seemed believable enough to get you going into the story. Sometimes the story feels a little bit linear and forced upon you, e.g. pages that you need to look into for information will sometimes be spoonfed to you. but I get it though, if it wasn't though, many people won't know what to do next and get stuck, and they will need to add a lot more useless filler pages/information to make it a more realistic and harder experience. As typical with these kinds of games, there are multiple endings, all affected by your choices in the game. so it adds a bit of replay value.

I only hope they add more episodes/cases next, as the story is a bit short and there is potential for more storytelling using the Orwell system, I also hope they added in voice acting for the voice call tapping parts. so It feels even more authentic. 

I'd also not recommend it for it's full price at the moment(IF they add in more free episodes/cases, then I will change my stance about this, a Season Two is coming though, but that's for another price unfortunately). if you can get it for 50% off, I'd say it's now worth it. For me, I got it in a humble bundle monthly subscription that gives around $200 worth of good games for around $12 a month, along with Rise of the Tomb Raider and other more games.

Score: 7/10

review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

P.S. Once you exit Orwell, you are greeted by advertisement of a sequel - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength. Fear not though, Keeping an Eye On You provides a complete storyline, no “to be continued” ending attached.

review_text_raw:
I've been wanting to write a short but to the point review for this game. Mostly because I rarely finish any games in one go. 

Orwell is [b]NOT[/b] going to WOW you. It's not mindblowing, mind you. It will, however, keep you intrigued once you decide to give it a try. 

[u]What's it about?[/u]

It's heavily influenced by the reveals of Edward Snowden. It's about working in the NSA and uncovering personal data in order to get to the truth. It's about whether or not as people we'd sacrifice our "freedom" or our "safety". Overall, an interesting premise.

[u]Right. It's a game, so what's the gameplay like?[/u]

The "game" consists of reading a lot of text and putting certain bits of it together in order to progress to the next chapters. It doesn't sound too engaging but once you start reading through it, it is able to drag you into its universe. There are multiple endings and choices where you need to choose what to reveal for the people you gather information yourself. 

[u]Multiple choices. Does that mean there's a lot of replayability?[/u]

Well, once you get to the conclusion, you sort of feel fulfilled, hence why many of the reviewers of this game have a few hours of gametime. [b]BUT[/b] I think you can easily play the game a second time to do a few things differently. There is some replayability potential.

Good soundtrack, interesting premise, amusing characters, nice artstyle, engaging storyline. I strongly recommend this game if you want something different.

review_text_raw: Orwell is OKAY. Not great, but I enjoyed the experience for what it was; a visual novel. To be frank, the story basically plays itself out. You're just a passenger in this ride. The actual simulation of being an "investigator" is not fulfilled here whatsoever. Everything you can take note of is already highlighted for you. This is the gaming equivalent of sticking wooden blocks in their appropriate holes. It's a shame a political story as convoluted and detailed as Orwell's is matched with mindless "gameplay". I enjoyed the unique approach to storytelling and seeing the plot unravel with many twists and turns was engrossing. However, having your advisor constantly chime in after every single datachunk is submitted is annoying and unnecessary. There's no in-depth deduction system like the Sherlock Holmes games. Everything is filled in and connected for you. I find the topics of surveillance, civil unrest, immigration, etc. very fascinating, but to have the game straight up tell you what the right and wrong choices are takes away from the experience imo. I don't need the game to wag its finger at me for deciding that the terrorists belong in prison. The lack of nuance in how your very few choices are reflected in the end feels patronizing. In reality, with or without Orwell, there would be massive consequences. It's a very complex discussion, but the game ends before any discussion can really be had rushing through the final episode with a sloppy "I think we should do this, BUT IT'S UP TO YOU [insert player name here]!" choice at the end that just feels unearned. The concept and strong premise drew me in and the mystery kept me to the end. If you value deep forensics gameplay, look elsewhere. If you want a fairly compelling political thriller, this is not bad for the price. (6/10)

review_text_raw:
[b]Believable writing and gameplay mesh to bring the Orwellian nightmare to life.[/b]

[u][i]Summary:[/i][/u]
With [i]Orwell[/i] literally simulating a job, its success or failure as a game almost entirely hinges on the strength of its writing. Fortunately for all of us, it succeeds with flying colors. The characters it depicts are distinct and memorable. The scenarios it presents to you demand your full attention, else you miss something that leads to catastrophe. In the end it will leave you wondering how else things could have played out.

To be clear, [i]Orwell[/i] is an almost entirely text based experience. It mimics a work computer, including internet browser, email, and even a news and weather report. There is no voice acting, though the voice in my head for each of them is so strong that I had to pause and double check myself on that. Props again to the writers for that. The sound in the game sets a good atmosphere but is limited in quantity to the point of being noticeably repetitive.

If you can stomach the reading load, [i]Orwell[/i] is a novel game that is well worth your time and the cost of admission.

[u][i]Additional details:[/i][/u]
The visual style of [i]Orwell[/i] does an excellent job of being familiar enough to reality while also smoothing over reality's rough edges and mismatching designs. Throughout the game you'll uncover multiple pictures of the same character, often showing different sides of the person than you've seen before. For example you may first discover a finely manicured business photo before later discovering a photo of the same person out on the town, presumably a few drinks in and having a good time. Of course these aren't real photos, but artist renditions.

In order to discuss this next topic, I'll give you the most basic, spoiler free description of what you do in the game. You are tasked with investigating specific people and deciding whether what you find does or does not get added to a government database. Essentially you are both the spy and the filter between your target and the government. With that said, there were a few instances related to this that hampered my immersion. Generally it came from being required to enter a piece of information into the Big Brother system that I would have elected to keep private had it not been needed to progress.

I'll close with a few words on replayability. While there are multiple endings and outcomes to each chapter, I personally didn't feel compelled to replay more than a couple specific moments. The decisions that lead to each result are rarely obvious, so it's hard to go back and change things without reexamining things on a larger scale than I was interested in. There are guides out there that could speed up the process if you're so interested. I happily spent 9 hours with [i]Orwell[/i], nearly all of which was a single careful playthrough.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is an investigative game akin to a visual novel. You play as The Investigator, someone whose job it is to use the powerful Orwell surveillance system to solve crimes – or in this case, solve a particular crime. You see, a bomb was set off in Freedom Plaza in The Nation, killing three people, and it is your job to try and catch the bomber before they can kill anyone else.

Orwell is more like an interactive novel than an ordinary video game – the game is wholly centered around reading text for about four and a half hours, and while it has more meaningful interaction than most visual novels, the actual gameplay itself is very simple and not very action-oriented. It is a very cerebral experience, and if reading lots of text isn’t your cup of tea, this is not the game for you.

You start out with a single person of interest – a young woman who left the Plaza shortly before the bomb went off. She was a protester who had been arrested for attacking a police officer, but who wasn’t prosecuted for it due to lack of evidence. It quickly becomes clear that not all is as it seems, and it seems unlikely that she personally was the bomber – but she has past associations with a group known as Thought, an anti-government group which often engages in extremist rhetoric. But are they really the sort of people who would kill people? Or are they just innocent bystanders coincidentally caught up in the investigation?

Orwell is a very ambiguous game, and it is precisely this ambiguity which really makes the game work. Thought is upset about living in a surveillance state, but it is clear from your perspective as The Investigator that the system is designed to be humane in many ways – the investigator passes on information to someone else, whose job it is to analyze the data. You cannot investigate people who aren’t targets – unless someone has been designated as suspicious by actual data, you cannot collect data at all them, nor are you allowed to go snooping through their things. But if they are a target of interest, you have nigh unlimited authority to go snooping. And while the state is clearly a bit authoritarian, it is also clear that the system works – crime has gone down, and you can catch several criminals over the course of the game who really did do bad things. The person on the other end, who helps to determine whether or not the data is really indicative of wrongdoing, is a genuinely nice person who cares about people and who urges you to collect more data. The leader of The Nation appears to genuinely be trying to help out neighboring states.

But all of this is muddied with the ambiguity of the fact that not everyone in the government is nice, and the general sinister nature of your surveillance. Your actions do have consequences, and it is clear that if you made the wrong decisions, you could potentially feed people bad data and get people put in jail – and the choice of whether or not to feed people bad data, and the impression you leave the government on people, is dependent on what data you give them.

The game, thus, is a combination of an investigation and a moral choice system – you are not only investigating who might be the bomber, but also deciding what is and is not relevant, what should and should not be part of the investigation, and you have the power to wrongfully put people in jail or put people in danger. The very simple gameplay of choosing what pieces of highlighted information to put into a database from various documents, webpages, emails, and phone and text conversations thus takes on a great deal of weight, and makes you think about what you’re doing in a very different way from other investigatory games, as you think of it not only in terms of true/false, but also whether the information morally belongs in the hands of the government.

And it puts stress on the player as well – you cannot take back your actions, so if you incorrectly present someone as a dangerous criminal, you can’t fix it and have to live with the consequences.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It’s timely that Orwell, the first game from Australian start-up Osmotic Studios delves into the muddy waters of government surveillance of its citizens, with the increasing nature of real world democracies doing the very same as they grapple with a world that is always connected and communicating.

Orwell opens with a deadly bombing in a public square that the player is tasked to investigate. This is achieved via a secret program codenamed Orwell, which allows an anonymous user, with the oversight of a supervisor, to snoop through social media posts, personal computers, bank statements and private correspondence of the suspects and associates.

My initial surveillance began with a singular suspect who had been caught by CCTV in the surrounding area and who had previously been arrested for attacking a police officer. My supervisor seemed to believe in this system, that malice lurked in unseen corners and that everyone was a potential threat.

From this one suspect a deeper conspiracy of activists emerged, and concerns of the erosion of liberties that were taken for granted by the citizens both fortified and weakened the idea of Orwell.

Continuing to spy on the fellow member’s activist group Thought reveals snippets of conversation that follow a story of mistrust of government and the over-reach of surveillance. Your actions, and inaction can and do have major consequences for those that you survey – and decisions on what you choose to upload to Orwell through a simple drag and drop interface can have fatal consequences and lock you to certain storylines.

Sifting through the large amount of data that the unknowing citizens freely make available reveals a story of love, betrayal, anger and sacrifice. I could have skipped this text – foregone most of the pertinent information. Highlighted text makes it easy to ascertain what is applicable to your current investigations. But this is to the game’s detriment – and the story woven is well worth your time.

Orwell paints a plausible microcosm of our online habits, with mirrors of Facebook, Twitter and chat logs providing a certain narcissistic perspective of how we perceive the world. These characters are fleshed out people, and the media puppet is scathingly presented as acting only in its self-interest. This is hilariously presented at moments, such as when it gives nothing by positive press to a major advertiser, even when your own investigations show there is moral outrage at their actions.

The highlighted information well can occasionally dry up, and you might have to recheck what you missed, but the six hour journey is worth the effort. Minor shortcomings in its design aside, Orwell provides a relatively gripping story of interactive fiction where whatever you upload, even the most trivial, can change the course of the story and of your understanding of it.

Orwell highlights the overarching issue of the choice between liberty and intrusion and how that plays out can weigh heavily on the decisions you make throughout the game. Something as minor as anxiety medication that is snooped from a suspect’s medical files leads the suspect to be targeted as unstable. It’s only a small leap from there to classify them as dangerous. We have nothing to fear if we have nothing to hide – and the ability to be able to follow these disparate people, through their online social interactions is a fascinating journey that I am really glad I took. 

The dilemma of authority versus autonomy shifts rapidly in a world that is under threat - and a game like Orwell, an interactive fiction no less, shows there is a lot more about us online than we may realise or care to know. Indeed, by the game’s end I was questioning what I knew about what information I had freely shared. That Orwell can have you re-examine your life is a testament to the present reality. It’s a great game, and well worth your time.

8.2/10.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is only getting more relevant in the years since it’s release given it’s subject matter of government surveillance. It is kind of a visual novel puzzle game where you navigate different platforms finding bits of info that you can tag to the database which in turn can find you more info. As you go on you start to unravel a story of who was behind the bombings. The bits of info are highlighted so you can’t miss them and you also don’t always have to tag them. This is because some info is out of context. For instance someone saying that they are being tortured by cupcakes is obviously not actual torture but you can still tag the person involved as a torturer. Having the discretion is nice but there are other times where you have to tag certain data to progress that I don’t feel was data that must have been tagged or as relevant as the game made it. I also don’t like how you can’t untag data. I also felt that at the end of the game there was supposed to be multiple ways to handle the outcome but I could only see one or possibly two. I don’t know why the other ways weren’t available to me as I can’t think of a story reason that I shouldn’t have been able to pull off what i wanted. The story was good but the twists near the end were simply fantastic. The UI for the game was easy to get used to and had a good design. I also liked how new parts of the software were revealed as they became needed. The game has no voice acting but that wasn’t an issue wand made sense given the fact that outside of recorded calls this was all  just you at a computer. The puzzle aspect was that you have to scour the various blogs; calls; emails; etc to find info you can use to further the game as well as provide additional depth details and context. 

	I played Orwell on Linux. It froze on me once but other than that I encountered no issues and noticed no spelling errors. There are no graphics options and the game has a 60 FPS cap. You can save on exit but there is just one save slot so you can’t undo choices or have multiple save files. Performance was good with no noticeable lag. Alt-Tab Didn’t work.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a truly amazing game. It really gets you thinking about mass surveillance. It's hardly impartial, but you get to see both the good and the bad aspects. If you have an interest in privacy, play this game. If you have never given it much thought, play this game. If you've ever said 'I have nothing to hide, it doesn't matter', play this game.

Pros:
- really gets you thinking about mass surveillance
- you control how the story unfolds based on what information you pass on to the government
- the story has some really great twists and surprises that I didn't see coming

Cons:
- Playing involves dragging and dropping pieces of information onto profiles of people you're investigating, but sometimes the drag and drop function is finicky, I occasionally had to retry multiple times to grab a piece of data. Not a big issue, but a minor annoyance.

A warning to achievement hunters: *do not* look at any 100% achievement guides before playing, they will ruin the story. You'll need 2 playthroughs anyway. Just play through normally the first time and you should be able to get all remaining achievements the second time.

Verdict: 10/10
